title.text: Leaving a vehicle on the road

why_how.text: Leaving a stalled vehicle the right way keeps it, and you, out of the path of traffic.

scenario.text: Ray's car stalls on a highway with a wide shoulder.

reasoning.text: He pulls onto the shoulder as far from traffic as he can, sets the parking brake, shifts into park and turns off the engine.

result.text: He puts out emergency signals and stays with the car until help arrives.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking it is fine to leave the engine running and walk off with the car unlocked.

correction.text: Switch off the engine before leaving the vehicle, and lock it if you have to walk away.

memory_support.text: Pull off, park it, signal, stay or lock.

prompt.text: Your car breaks down on a highway shoulder. After securing it, what should you do if possible?

answer.text: Put out emergency signals and stay with the vehicle until help arrives.

rationale.text: The manual asks you to set out proper emergency signals and, when you can, wait with the vehicle for help.

title.text: When you must leave your car

lines.text: Pull as far off as you can.
Signal and stay, or lock it.

narration.text: This lesson begins the section on parking and freeway driving with a situation every driver may face: having to leave a vehicle on a highway or street. Here is where to put it. If you must leave your vehicle on a highway or street, pull onto the shoulder as far from traffic as you can, or as close to the curb as possible where there is one. Then we look at how to secure it, how to warn other drivers, whether to stay, and what to do if you must walk away. Each step keeps the stopped vehicle from becoming a hazard. In short: Pull as far off as you can; secure the vehicle; signal and stay, or lock it.

lines.text: Park, or a manual left in gear.

narration.text: Once the car is as far from traffic as you can get it, make sure it cannot move. Before leaving it, set the parking brake, shift into park or leave a manual transmission in gear, and switch off the engine. Those three actions, the brake, the gear and the engine, work together so the vehicle stays exactly where you left it. Each of the three steps on its own helps, and together they keep the vehicle from rolling or starting while you are away from it. In short: Set the parking brake; park, or a manual left in gear; engine off.

lines.text: Stay with the vehicle if possible.

narration.text: Next, make sure other drivers know the car is there. Put out proper emergency signals and, if possible, stay with the vehicle until help arrives. Staying with the vehicle, when you can, keeps you near the car while you wait for help instead of out along the road. Proper emergency signals are what let approaching drivers see the stopped vehicle in time. Staying with it is the choice the manual prefers whenever that is possible, until help arrives. In short: Put out emergency signals; stay with the vehicle if possible; wait until help arrives.

lines.text: If you must leave, lock it.

narration.text: Here is a step people skip in a hurry. If you have to walk away from the vehicle, lock it. Pair that with the earlier steps: the engine is off, the parking brake is set, the gear is in park or held in gear, and the emergency signals are out. Only then do you walk away, and you lock the vehicle before you go. In short: If you must leave, lock it; engine off first; signals already out. Remember: Before leaving it, set the parking brake, shift into park or leave a manual transmission in gear, and switch off the engine.

lines.text: The car is secured on the shoulder.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: your car breaks down, and you have pulled it onto the shoulder and secured it. What should you do next, if possible? The answer is to put out emergency signals and stay with the vehicle until help arrives. Put out proper emergency signals and, if possible, stay with the vehicle until help arrives. If you must walk away instead, lock the vehicle first. If you have to walk away from the vehicle, lock it. Signals out, and wait with the car. Securing the vehicle comes first, then the signals, then waiting with it if you can.

lines.text: Shoulder or curb, far from traffic.

narration.text: To close, if you must leave your vehicle on a highway or street, pull onto the shoulder as far from traffic as you can, or as close to the curb as possible. Set the parking brake, shift into park or leave a manual transmission in gear, and switch off the engine. Put out proper emergency signals and, if possible, stay with the vehicle until help arrives. If you have to walk away from it, lock it. Those steps keep both you and other drivers safe. In short: Shoulder or curb, far from traffic; brake, gear, engine off; signals out; stay or lock.

why_how.text: Illegal parking can block traffic, hide pedestrians and slow emergency crews, so Arizona lists where parking is banned.

scenario.text: Lena looks for a spot near a corner with a crosswalk, a fire hydrant and railroad tracks nearby.

reasoning.text: She must stay at least twenty feet from the crosswalk, fifteen feet from the hydrant and fifty feet from the tracks.

result.text: She finds a space that clears all three distances and has no signs banning parking.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking one no-parking distance covers hydrants, crosswalks and railroad crossings.

correction.text: The distances differ: fifteen feet from a fire hydrant, twenty feet from a crosswalk at an intersection, and fifty feet from a railroad crossing.

memory_support.text: Fifteen hydrant, twenty crosswalk, fifty tracks.

prompt.text: You want to park near a railroad crossing. How far away must you be?

rationale.text: Parking within fifty feet of a railroad crossing is illegal, a longer distance than the hydrant and crosswalk rules.

narration.text: This lesson lists the places where parking is against the law. Start with three everyday spots. Parking is illegal on a sidewalk, in front of any public or private driveway, and inside the boundaries of an intersection. We will then cover crosswalks, freeways, signs and hazards, the measured distances from hydrants and railroad crossings, and bridges and tunnels. Several of these rules use numbers, so pay attention to which number goes with which place. In short: Sidewalks, driveways, intersections; crosswalks and nearby; freeways, bridges and tunnels.

lines.text: Twenty feet from an intersection crosswalk.

narration.text: Crosswalks get extra room. Parking is illegal on a crosswalk, and also anywhere closer than twenty feet to a crosswalk at an intersection. Signs and safety also decide where you may park. You may not park where signs prohibit it or in any way that creates a hazard for other vehicles. So even a spot that is not on the list can be illegal if a sign bans parking or if your car would endanger other vehicles. Signs win. In short: No parking on a crosswalk; twenty feet from an intersection crosswalk; obey signs; create no hazard.

lines.text: Fifteen feet from a fire hydrant.
Fifty feet from a railroad crossing.

narration.text: Two more distances matter. Parking within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant is illegal. Parking within fifty feet of a railroad crossing is illegal. And some places ban parking outright. You may not park on a bridge or inside a tunnel. Each of these rules stands on its own. The fifteen-foot hydrant rule and the fifty-foot railroad rule are measured distances, while the bridge and tunnel rule bans parking on the structure itself, with no distance to measure. In short: Fifteen feet from a fire hydrant; fifty feet from a railroad crossing; bridges and tunnels: never.

Here is the trap. Because these distances look alike, people swap them or assume one number covers everything. The no-parking distances differ by object: fifteen feet from a fire hydrant, twenty feet from a crosswalk at an intersection, and fifty feet from a railroad crossing. A good check is the order from smallest to largest: the hydrant comes first, then the crosswalk at an intersection, then the railroad crossing. In short: Hydrant: fifteen feet; crosswalk: twenty feet; railroad crossing: fifty feet. Remember: Parking within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant is illegal.

Freeways have their own rule. Parking on any freeway or interstate highway is illegal except in an emergency. An emergency does not excuse the safety steps, either. Freeway parking is banned except for emergencies, and an emergency stop still calls for the shoulder, the brake, the engine off and warning signals. So even when you must stop, you still use the shoulder and secure the vehicle the way the first lesson described. In short: No freeway or interstate parking; except in an emergency; emergency stops still have steps.

lines.text: How far away must you be?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you want to park near a railroad crossing. How far away must you be? The answer is at least fifty feet. Parking within fifty feet of a railroad crossing is illegal. That is the longest of the three distances in this lesson. The no-parking distances differ by object: fifteen feet from a fire hydrant, twenty feet from a crosswalk at an intersection, and fifty feet from a railroad crossing. If you said fifteen or twenty feet, you were thinking of the hydrant or the crosswalk rule. Fifty feet for tracks.

To sum up, parking is illegal on a sidewalk, in front of any public or private driveway, inside an intersection, on a crosswalk, and closer than twenty feet to a crosswalk at an intersection. It is also illegal within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant, within fifty feet of a railroad crossing, on a bridge or in a tunnel, where signs prohibit it, or in any way that creates a hazard. Parking on any freeway or interstate is illegal except in an emergency, and an emergency stop still follows the usual safety steps. In short: Sidewalks, driveways, intersections, crosswalks; fifteen, twenty, fifty feet; no freeways, bridges or tunnels.

why_how.text: Freeways carry fast traffic, so smooth merging and careful exits prevent sudden conflicts.

scenario.text: Omar drives up an on-ramp toward busy freeway traffic.

reasoning.text: He matches the speed of the right lane, signals, checks around him and merges once it is clear.

result.text: He stays inside the lines on the ramp, never crossing the solid line or the gore area.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking traffic already on the freeway must make room for you.

correction.text: Drivers entering a freeway must yield to traffic already on it and are responsible for merging safely.

prompt.text: What is the order of steps for merging onto a freeway?

answer.text: Match the right lane's speed, signal, check traffic and merge carefully when clear.

rationale.text: Merging means matching the right lane's speed, while exiting uses a deceleration lane to slow down.

lines.text: Exits need signals and smooth braking.

narration.text: This lesson covers getting onto and off a freeway. Here is why freeways deserve care. Freeways and interstate highways are built to carry higher-speed traffic safely. The rules for entering and exiting are designed around that speed. We will look at who yields, how to merge, the lines you must not cross, and how to exit smoothly, including in heavy traffic. Each step in this lesson connects to that speed. Speed is the theme. In short: Freeways carry higher-speed traffic; entering drivers yield; exits need signals and smooth braking.

lines.text: Traffic on the freeway goes first.

narration.text: Here is the first rule of entering. Drivers entering a freeway must yield to the traffic already on it and are responsible for merging safely. That puts the job of fitting in on you, the driver coming up the ramp. Traffic already on the freeway has the priority, and your task is to find a safe place among it. Yielding on entry is a duty for the driver on the ramp, not for the traffic already moving on the freeway. The ramp driver yields. In short: Entering drivers yield; Traffic on the freeway goes first; you are responsible for merging.

Here is the merging routine. To merge, match your speed to the traffic in the freeway's right lane, signal, check the traffic around you and merge carefully once it is clear. Matching speed is the key part, and the manual names the right lane as the speed to match. Signaling and checking the traffic around you come next, and the merge itself happens only once it is clear. The right lane is where you join, so its speed is the one you match before you move over. In short: Match the right lane's speed; signal and check around you; merge carefully when clear.

Here is a mistake drivers make when they are in a hurry to merge or exit. While entering a freeway, do not cross a solid line or drive through a gore area. The manual repeats the rule for both directions. A solid line is off-limits both when entering and when exiting a freeway, and so is the gore area on entry. So stay inside the lane lines on ramps, whether you are coming or going. A solid line on a ramp is a firm boundary in both directions of travel. In short: No solid line on entry; no gore area on entry; no solid line on exit.

lines.text: Brake properly for a smooth exit.

narration.text: Leaving the freeway has its own steps. Signal before you exit a freeway. Most freeways have deceleration lanes to help you exit, and proper braking gives a smooth exit. On entry you match the speed of the freeway right lane, while on exit most freeways give you a deceleration lane in which to brake smoothly. The signal comes first, then the move into the deceleration lane, and the braking happens there rather than in the travel lanes. In short: Signal before you exit; use the deceleration lane; brake properly for a smooth exit.

lines.text: Do not cross a solid line.

narration.text: Heavy traffic adds two cautions. When exiting in heavy traffic, keep a space cushion behind the vehicle ahead and do not cross a solid line. So when the exit lane is crowded, leave room in front of you and stay in your lane rather than cutting across lines at the last moment. The space cushion gives you room if the vehicle ahead slows, and staying behind the solid line keeps you out of the path of other exiting drivers. Room ahead, lines respected. In short: Keep a space cushion ahead; do not cross a solid line; stay patient in the lane.

Here is a quick check: you are coming up an on-ramp onto a busy freeway. What are the steps for merging? The answer is to match the speed of the right lane, signal, check the traffic around you and merge carefully once it is clear. To merge, match your speed to the traffic in the freeway's right lane, signal, check the traffic around you and merge carefully once it is clear. Remember the difference on the way off: there you signal and slow down in the deceleration lane. On entry you match the speed of the freeway right lane, while on exit most freeways give you a deceleration lane in which to brake smoothly.

lines.text: Yield and match speed to merge.
No solid lines or gore area.
Signal and brake smoothly to exit.

narration.text: To close, freeways and interstate highways are built for higher-speed traffic. Entering drivers yield to traffic already on the freeway and are responsible for merging safely: match the right lane's speed, signal, check traffic and merge once it is clear. Do not cross a solid line or drive through a gore area while entering. Signal before you exit, use the deceleration lane and brake properly for a smooth exit, and in heavy traffic keep a space cushion and do not cross a solid line. In short: Yield and match speed to merge; no solid lines or gore area; signal and brake smoothly to exit.

why_how.text: Knowing how highways are built and how each lane is used helps you choose the right lane early and recover safely from a missed exit.

scenario.text: Grace realizes too late that her exit was the one she just passed.

reasoning.text: She does not stop or back up on the highway.

result.text: She leaves at the next exit and follows the signs to rejoin the road going the other way.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may back up along the shoulder if you miss an exit by a little.

correction.text: A missed exit is handled by driving on to the next exit and following signs back, never by stopping or reversing.

memory_support.text: Missed it? Next exit, never reverse.

prompt.text: You just passed your exit on the highway. What is the right way to get back?

answer.text: Leave at the next exit and follow the signs to rejoin the road going the other way.

rationale.text: You never stop or back up after a missed exit; the next exit is the way back.

narration.text: This lesson covers how highways are laid out and how to use their lanes. Here is the first type. A divided highway or freeway has separate roadways for the two directions, often with several lanes on each side. And here is how controlled-access highways differ. Some highways meet other roads at traffic signals, while controlled-access highways have no signals or intersections and are entered and left only by ramps; these are called expressways or freeways. We will then cover getting into the right lane early, signaling and joining, missed exits, and how the lanes are used on multi-lane roads.

lines.text: Get into the proper lane in advance.
Yield and match speed when joining.

narration.text: Preparation makes highway moves safe. Get into the proper lane well in advance so you can enter or leave the highway safely. Signal your exit before you reach the exit ramp. When joining a highway, yield to drivers already on it and speed up to match their speed as you enter the travel lane. Getting into the right lane early, signaling before the ramp, and yielding and matching speed when joining are three parts of the same preparation. In short: Get into the proper lane in advance; signal before the exit ramp; yield and match speed when joining.

lines.text: Take the next exit and come back.

narration.text: Every driver misses an exit sometimes. If you miss your exit, do not stop and never back up; leave at the next exit and follow the signs to rejoin the road going the other way. The freeway rules say the same. If you miss a freeway exit, do not back up; you must go on to the next exit. So a missed exit has one safe answer: keep going to the next exit, then follow the signs back to the road going the other way. The next exit is always the way back, even when the missed exit is close behind you. In short: Do not stop; never back up; take the next exit and come back.

Here is the trap. A missed exit just a short way back tempts drivers to stop or reverse along the shoulder. A missed exit is handled by driving on to the next exit and following signs back, never by stopping or reversing. The few minutes lost by going on to the next exit are part of the rule, not a reason to break it. In short: Missed exit: keep going; no stopping, no backing; next exit, then signs back. Remember: If you miss your exit, do not stop and never back up; leave at the next exit and follow the signs to rejoin the road going the other way.

On multi-lane roads, lane position follows a basic rule. On any road with two or more lanes, drive on the right half except when passing or when signs say otherwise. So your normal place is on the right half of the road, and you move left only to pass or where signs direct you. Passing is the main reason to leave the right half, along with signs that direct you elsewhere. Keeping to the right half is the normal position on any road with two or more lanes. In short: Drive on the right half; pass on the left; follow signs that say otherwise.

lines.text: At rush hour, through drivers may avoid it.

narration.text: On bigger highways the right lane behaves differently. On highways with three or more lanes in one direction, the right lane usually serves entering and exiting traffic, so it may move slower or faster than the other lanes. The right lane of a highway with three or more lanes can carry traffic both slower and faster than the other lanes, because it serves entering and exiting vehicles. At rush hour, drivers who are not exiting may want to stay out of the right lane to leave room for vehicles entering and leaving. In short: Serves entering and exiting traffic; can be slower or faster; at rush hour, through drivers may avoid it.

Here is a quick check: you just passed your exit on the highway. What is the right way to get back? The answer is to leave at the next exit and follow the signs to rejoin the road going the other way. If you miss your exit, do not stop and never back up; leave at the next exit and follow the signs to rejoin the road going the other way. Stopping or backing up is never the answer. A missed exit is handled by driving on to the next exit and following signs back, never by stopping or reversing. Stopping or backing up is never the answer after a missed exit.

lines.text: Plan your lane early; signal before the ramp.
Missed exit: next exit, never reverse.
Keep right; watch merges; no tailgating.

narration.text: To close, a divided highway has separate roadways for each direction, and controlled-access highways, called expressways or freeways, have no signals or intersections and use ramps. Get into the proper lane well in advance, signal before the exit ramp, and when joining, yield and speed up to match traffic. If you miss your exit, never stop or back up; go on to the next exit and follow the signs back. Drive on the right half except to pass, expect the right lane on bigger highways to serve entering and exiting traffic, watch for merging vehicles, signal, keep within limits and do not tailgate.

why_how.text: The gore area and freeway breakdowns are both places where a stopped or slow car can be struck, so the rules keep you out of harm's way.

scenario.text: Mae's car starts to overheat on the freeway at night.

reasoning.text: She pulls as far as she can onto the right shoulder, away from the ramps, and turns on her flashers and the inside dome light.

result.text: She waits with her car instead of walking along the freeway.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the gore area is a safe place to pull over when you need help.

correction.text: Driving over or parking on any part of the gore area is against the law; pull onto the right shoulder away from the ramps instead.

memory_support.text: Right shoulder, flashers, wait with the car.

prompt.text: It is dark and your car is disabled on the freeway shoulder. What can you add to your flashers to signal for help?

answer.text: The inside dome light, or flares or portable warning signals.

rationale.text: After dark, the manual adds the dome light or flares and portable warning signals to the daytime flashers or raised hood.

lines.text: Stopping for help on a freeway.

narration.text: This lesson covers two freeway situations: the gore area beside every ramp, and what to do when you need help. Here is the gore area rule. Driving over or parking on any part of a gore area, the space between a through roadway and an entrance or exit ramp, is against the law. Then we look at where to stop when you need help, how to signal for it by day and at night, what to do while you wait, and how to pass someone else's disabled vehicle. In short: What a gore area is; stopping for help on a freeway; passing a disabled vehicle.

lines.text: The gore area is a wedge by the ramp.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The gore area can look like extra space, and drivers drift across it or stop there. A gore area is the wedge between the through road and a ramp; driving over it and parking in it are both against the law. So if you need to stop, the gore area is not the place. The next slide shows where to go instead. In short: The gore area is a wedge by the ramp; no driving over it; no parking on it. Remember: Driving over or parking on any part of a gore area, the space between a through roadway and an entrance or exit ramp, is against the law.

lines.text: As far onto the right shoulder as you can.

narration.text: Here is the right place. If you need help on a freeway, pull as far as you can onto the right shoulder and avoid stopping on or near the ramps. Keeping away from the ramps keeps you out of the path of traffic entering and leaving the freeway, and the far edge of the right shoulder puts the most distance between you and the travel lanes. The far edge of the right shoulder is the safest place the manual names. Away from the ramps, as far right as you can. In short: As far onto the right shoulder as you can; away from the ramps; not in the gore area.

Other drivers need to know you are there. To signal for help, turn on your emergency flashers or raise the hood; after dark, switch on the inside dome light or set out flares or portable warning signals. By day you signal for freeway help with flashers or a raised hood, while after dark you add the dome light or flares and portable warning signals. Flashers or a raised hood by day, and the dome light or flares and portable warning signals after dark, are the signals the manual lists. In short: Flashers or a raised hood; after dark: dome light; or flares and warning signals.

lines.text: Do not walk along the freeway.
Slow, move over and pass carefully.

narration.text: Two more rules cover the waiting and the other side of the situation. Wait for help with your vehicle and do not walk along the freeway. When you come upon a disabled vehicle on the freeway, slow down, move over and pass around it with caution. Waiting with the vehicle keeps you off the freeway on foot, and when you are the one passing, slowing down and moving over gives the stopped vehicle room. Both rules protect people outside a moving car. In short: Wait with your vehicle; do not walk along the freeway; slow, move over and pass carefully.

lines.text: Disabled on the shoulder at night.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: it is dark and your car is disabled on the freeway shoulder. What can you add to your flashers to signal for help? The answer is the inside dome light, or flares or portable warning signals. To signal for help, turn on your emergency flashers or raise the hood; after dark, switch on the inside dome light or set out flares or portable warning signals. By day, flashers or a raised hood are the signals the manual names. By day you signal for freeway help with flashers or a raised hood, while after dark you add the dome light or flares and portable warning signals.

lines.text: Stay out of the gore area.
Signal, wait, and pass others carefully.

narration.text: To finish, a gore area is the space between a through roadway and an entrance or exit ramp, and driving over or parking on any part of it is against the law. If you need help on a freeway, pull as far as you can onto the right shoulder and avoid stopping on or near the ramps. Signal with your flashers or a raised hood, and after dark with the dome light or flares and portable warning signals. Wait with your vehicle instead of walking along the freeway, and when you pass a disabled vehicle, slow down, move over and pass with caution.

why_how.text: HOV lanes move car pools, motorcycles and buses faster at busy times, and breaking the rule brings substantial fines.

scenario.text: Ben drives to work on a weekday during the posted HOV hours with a coworker in the passenger seat.

reasoning.text: With himself counted, the car carries two persons, so it may use the HOV lane.

result.text: He signals and takes care as he crosses the solid white line into the lane.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the driver does not count toward the two persons the HOV rule requires.

correction.text: The HOV rule counts the driver as one of the two persons required, and it applies only at the posted weekday times.

prompt.text: During posted weekday HOV hours, may a driver alone in a car use the HOV lane?

answer.text: No, the car needs at least two persons, counting the driver.

rationale.text: At the posted weekday times, vehicles with fewer than two persons, counting the driver, may not use the HOV lane.

narration.text: This lesson covers HOV lanes. Start with how to spot one. HOV lanes are marked by white diamonds painted in the roadway. We will then look at who may use the lane during its posted times, how the people in the car are counted, the penalty for breaking the rule, and how to move into and out of the lane safely. Each rule applies only while the lane is restricted. The diamonds tell you the lane has its own rules, and the posted times tell you when those rules apply. In short: Marked by white diamonds; rules at posted weekday times; fines for violations.

lines.text: Two or more persons, counting the driver.

narration.text: Here is the occupancy rule. At the posted times on weekdays, a vehicle carrying fewer than two persons, counting the driver, may not use an HOV lane, which is then reserved for car pools, motorcycles and buses. The allowed vehicles are listed together. Car pools, motorcycles and buses may use an HOV lane during restricted times, and crossing its solid white line requires a signal. So during those posted times, a car pool with at least two persons, a motorcycle or a bus may use the lane. In short: Two or more persons, counting the driver; motorcycles and buses; at posted weekday times.

lines.text: The driver is one of them.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People think two persons means two passengers. The HOV rule counts the driver as one of the two persons required, and it binds only at the posted weekday times. So a driver with one passenger meets the rule, and outside the posted weekday times the restriction does not bind at all. In short: Two persons needed; the driver is one of them; only at posted times. Remember: At the posted times on weekdays, a vehicle carrying fewer than two persons, counting the driver, may not use an HOV lane, which is then reserved for car pools, motorcycles and buses.

lines.text: Signal across the solid white line.

narration.text: Breaking the rule is costly. A motorist who breaks the HOV restriction faces substantial fines and penalties. Moving into and out of the lane takes care too. Always signal and take care when crossing the solid white line into or out of an HOV lane. The solid white line marks the lane's edge, and you cross it only with a signal and attention to traffic. The fines are substantial, so check the posted times and count the people in the car before you move over. In short: Substantial fines and penalties; signal across the solid white line; take care entering and leaving.

lines.text: May the car use the lane?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: during the posted weekday HOV hours, may a driver alone in a car use the HOV lane? No. At the posted times on weekdays, a vehicle carrying fewer than two persons, counting the driver, may not use an HOV lane, which is then reserved for car pools, motorcycles and buses. The car needs at least two persons, and the driver counts as one of them. The HOV rule counts the driver as one of the two persons required, and it binds only at the posted weekday times. With one passenger aboard, the same car would qualify.

lines.text: Two persons, driver included, at posted times.

narration.text: To close, HOV lanes are marked by white diamonds painted in the roadway. At the posted times on weekdays, a vehicle carrying fewer than two persons, counting the driver, may not use the lane, which is reserved for car pools, motorcycles and buses. A motorist who breaks the restriction faces substantial fines and penalties. Always signal and take care when crossing the solid white line into or out of an HOV lane. In short: White diamonds mark the lane; two persons, driver included, at posted times; signal across the solid line.

why_how.text: Freeway rules ban the moves that put a driver across fast traffic, and good lane habits keep traffic flowing.

scenario.text: Ava drives a three-lane highway behind a slow truck in the far right lane.

reasoning.text: The far right lane is the slower through lane and the far left is the passing lane, so she signals and moves left to pass.

result.text: After passing she returns to the right, keeping right except to pass.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may park on the freeway shoulder whenever you need a break.

correction.text: Shoulder parking on a freeway is banned except in an emergency, and stopping is allowed only in areas specially provided.

memory_support.text: Keep right, pass left, stop only where provided.

prompt.text: On a three-lane highway, which lane does the manual treat as the passing lane?

rationale.text: On a three-lane highway, the far right lane is the slower through lane and the far left lane is the passing lane.

narration.text: This lesson closes the freeway topic with a set of firm rules. Start with what is never allowed. On a freeway, never drive over or across a median or divided-highway separation, and never make a U-turn. On a freeway, never change lanes without signaling, and get onto the freeway only by an on-ramp. After that we look at where you may stop, getting your vehicle ready for highway speeds, and how to use the lanes, including on a three-lane highway. In short: Things never to do; where you may stop; how to use the lanes.

Freeways have strict limits on stopping. Do not park or stop on a freeway except in areas provided for it; parking on the shoulder is banned except in an emergency. Shoulder parking on a freeway is banned except in an emergency, while stopping is allowed only in areas specially provided. So the only places to stop are the areas provided for it, and the shoulder is kept for real emergencies. Provided areas and emergencies are the only exceptions. In short: Only in provided areas; shoulder parking: emergencies only; no casual stops.

Here is the trap. A wide freeway shoulder looks like a handy place to stop for a phone call or a rest. It is not. The manual allows shoulder parking only in an emergency and stopping only in areas specially provided. So if you need a break, use a provided area, and keep the shoulder for real emergencies. In short: Shoulder parking: emergencies only; stop only in provided areas; otherwise keep moving. Remember: Shoulder parking on a freeway is banned except in an emergency, while stopping is allowed only in areas specially provided.

Before you even reach the freeway, the vehicle matters. Before highway driving, make sure your vehicle is in good operating condition and can keep up highway speeds. So the check covers two things: the vehicle's operating condition, and whether it can keep up highway speeds. Checking the vehicle before a highway trip is part of driving safely at highway speeds. Both parts of the check come before the trip, not after you are already on the freeway. In short: Good operating condition; able to keep highway speeds; check before you go.

lines.text: Keep right; left lane to pass.

narration.text: Lane choice follows a pattern. Keep right and use the left lane only to pass; on a three-lane highway, treat the far right lane as the slower through lane and the far left lane as the passing lane. On a three-lane highway the far right lane is treated as the slower through lane and the far left lane as the passing lane. Moving back to the right after passing keeps the far left lane free for others who need to pass. Keep right, pass left. In short: Keep right; left lane to pass; far right: slower through lane; far left: passing lane.

lines.text: Drive in the middle of your lane.
Mirror and signals for lane changes.

narration.text: Two final habits round out the section. Drive in the middle of your lane between the lines, and use your rearview mirror and turn signals when changing lanes. Traffic is controlled by signal lights, traffic signs and pavement markings, and you must fully understand them to drive safely. Staying centered between the lines, using the rearview mirror and signals for lane changes, and understanding signals, signs and markings all work together. In short: Drive in the middle of your lane; mirror and signals for lane changes; know signals, signs and markings.

Here is a quick check: on a three-lane highway, which lane does the manual treat as the passing lane? The answer is the far left lane. The far right lane is treated as the slower through lane. On a three-lane highway the far right lane is treated as the slower through lane and the far left lane as the passing lane. Keep right and move left only to pass.

lines.text: Keep right; middle of the lane.

narration.text: To sum up, on a freeway never drive across a median or make a U-turn, never change lanes without signaling, and get on only by an on-ramp. Do not park or stop except in areas provided for it, and park on the shoulder only in an emergency. Make sure your vehicle is in good operating condition and can keep up highway speeds. Keep right and use the left lane only to pass, drive in the middle of your lane with mirror checks and signals, and understand the signal lights, signs and pavement markings that control traffic.
